en: Of your dark-hearted prince,
The true son of the tiger,
Descendant of the mighty
Who smoked whenever he was spent
And grew fiercer whenever he died?
If you do not tell, suddenly,
When that desperate man’s anger rises,
A man’s affairs are perilous.
May he not stretch out the hair at your temples,
Or give you the divorce of a cast-off wife!
Do not be obstinate; hear my words.
My daughter-in-law, heed me now.
If you disobey and your sorrow boils,
He may put a kementei upon you,
Mount you on a bay mare,
And drive you toward your father.
When your father gave you,
When you came here as a bride,
You shone in a kete coat,
Rode proudly upon a bay pacer,
And shone in a supa coat,
And rode proudly on a gray pacer.
If you make trouble, my colt,
How will you depart,
Flapping in a kementei,
Swaggering on a bay mare?
Know that this would be a great shame.
How will you wander away,
Swaggering on a gray mare,
Flapping in a hide coat?
My child, heed these words of mine:
All the people blessed by Kydyr are here;
Dear old Bakay is here;
Sarykan of the bowl-shaped eyes,
The khan of sacred power, is here;
And Jamgyrchy, hero of the Esheks,
Is also here.”
When the senior wife said this,
The witless woman Chachykey
Now stood and seethed,
And spoke in an altogether different way
To the khans of the Esheks:
“Women who came as mediators,
Leave now, you wretches!
Dig your deep graves—
I shall boil your suffering!
You came here seeking support
From your sprawling elder Bakay.
I know all of you perfectly:
Your white-bearded old Bakay,
You three women, his playthings,
And your hairless bald man
Whom you sit worshiping as a saint.
I know what you are doing,
And the one you chose to bring,
Your witless, lowborn fellow
Called Jamgyrchy.
You old ones with swan-white beards—
May God strike all of you down!”
The poor woman did not know
That Bakay was listening nearby;
Beginning with Khan Bakay,
She cursed every one of them.
The three senior wives led the way
And fled outside in a rush,
Their necks stretching like geese,
Both cheeks turning red.
There was no cure to be found:
“She has insulted the khan,” they said,
And all pinched their own faces.
Old Bakay heard
Her vicious torrent of abuse,
And all that had been said.
Misery fell upon Bakay.
The three khans sat drooping,
Hunched like frozen camels,
Unable to die from shame,
Or enter the grave in death,
Unable to understand
What manner of woman this loud daughter-in-law was.
Since Bakay first became Bakay,
Since Bakay first mounted a horse,
Since he stretched himself and became a man,
Standing equal with the sons of heroes,
Since Bakay first mounted a horse
And became a pillar of the people,
He had never died when fate reached him;
Bakay was no woman,
Yet he had never seen such treatment from a man.
To witness this judgment-day affair,
To have his beard and head reviled—
It was the death of Khan Bakay.
Prince Bakay the tiger,
Who had mustered armies and struck the Kalmyks,
Your elder Prince Bakay,
Broke down and spoke in a low voice:
“In the time when our fortune remained safe,
When the tiger Manas lived,
Kara-Shaar and Kambyl—
When I had the Kalmyks surrounded,
And struck them with resounding blows,
While I was beating them,
Why did I not die there?
Alas, when Manas lived,
When the swaggering Kojo stood before me,
My hand could reach him.
When I faced Kakan and Keng-Tung,
And had them surrounded,
And was beating
The bald men of seething China,
Each carrying a stone,
Why did I not die there?
When my wise Manas lived,
When I cast turmoil
Across the face of the earth,
Whoever stood in defiance,
I seized and offered up,
And slaughtered him as a sacrifice,
Why did I not die there?
This life I live is an evil name.
My courser Manas, take me with you!”
Bakay stood and said these words.
Your dear woman Kanykey
Took gifts and pacers for the three khans,
And grasped a golden staff.
She cried out in fury
And summoned the two twins:
“Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
You whom I nursed in turn five times
Before the five Argakar stars had set—
By your fathers’ graves, you two wretches,
Has almighty God struck you?
Sink down never to be born,
Die rather than walk alive!
When a horse dies, wretches,
Its hide is needed;
When an elder brother dies, wretches,
A sister-in-law is needed.
When an elder brother loses his sight,
And his wife becomes unruly,
His younger brothers restrain her fury.
Go and gouge out her blinding eyes;
Slaughter as a sacrifice
The wretch who insulted the khan!
I myself shall face
Whatever calamity comes from it.
She and I were born together,
Our fortunes born equal;
I myself shall give the rival wife,
And whatever disaster follows,
I alone shall face it!”
She girded her waist belt,
Shouted in anger,
And summoned Kulchoro.
Taking the golden staff in hand,
She struck Kulchoro once.
Having taken a blow from his mother,
Capable Kulchoro—
He was a hero of twelve years;
Do not ask of his blazing ardor.
He seized the black-jawed whip,
Bent it double in his hand,
Forced his knee toward the ground,
And ran toward Chachykey
To tell what had become of the falcon,
And to call the foul-tongued woman
To account before returning.
When he drew near the fortress,
Chachykey’s forty daughters-in-law
Had fastened the gate
And stood holding the door.
He bellowed and shouted,
Calling, “Open the door!”
And Kulchoro now arrived.
At the door they had barred securely,
The brave-born Kulchoro
Struck, broke through, and entered.
He seized the woman by the buttocks,
With her forty daughters-in-law at their head,
And swooped upon her like a hawk.
Kulchoro was a tiger indeed:
Her poor hair, thick as sedge,
He gathered firmly in his hand.
The woman who had answered back
Kulchoro caught at once
And began lashing with resounding blows.
Her dress was torn apart,
Her fat rump laid bare,
And the dark blood driven from her
Poured down her sides.
Chachykey's forty daughters-in-law
All fled away shrieking:
"He has slaughtered our sister-in-law!" they cried,
All of them sobbing bitterly.
Her flesh split in pieces broad as platters;
Once the whip had struck her,
Her blood streamed down in rivulets.
Terrified, that sister-in-law of yours
Cried out and told the truth:
"She changed herself into a white swan,
And carried away the falcon.
Calling her 'the shrew Aychurok,'
I drew the fateful line;
That black-faced Aychurok
Has played this wondrous trick.
The elders know Churok;
She was the one who began the tumult.
Last night, on the holy night of Friday,
On the Thursday evening,
We stood casting stones at one another
And fought without yielding.
Aychurok flew out over the land,
Surely to test the thoroughbred,
And has carried away
Semetey's falcon."
I shall drive seven hundred red camels,
And livestock enough to cover the earth.
If I do not braid every tail,
If this year I do not behold
The face of Akun, to whom I am betrothed;
If I do not drive seven thousand
Bay horses as the sister-in-law's gift,
And well-fed gray camels
Whose trailing breast hair sweeps the ground;
He had a hand strong enough to take her,
And he was himself the khan of Afghanistan.
If I do not give them as her bride-price,
If this year I do not behold
The face of blessed Akun;
If I do not win for my hero Semetey
The noble-born Churok,
That serene beauty—
The knowing speak at length,
Saying, "Churok is the fairy's daughter";
The ignorant repeat tales,
Saying she has stirred turmoil
Throughout the whole wide world.
Those who beheld her beauty
Made claims upon Khan Akun
For Churok from every foreign land.
"Give us your grown daughter," they said;
None who heard the report let the matter rest,
And countless giants pressed their claims.
Even then, it was she
Who kept poor Akun's head unharmed.
Many times we conquered Afghanistan,
That sprawling black-walled city;
The great khan who gave his word
Possessed sacred authority.
Send my greetings to Semetey.
Tell him plainly, without reserve,
That his hero's Akshunkar
Was carried away
To the city of Akyn Khan.
That was Churok herself.
She changed herself into a white swan,
